rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the seventh and final Makkan sūrah in its group, closing the Makkan portion.
rows.anchor: This is the seventh sūrah of this group and on it ends its Makkan sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah sums up the reward-and-punishment discussion from Qāf through al-Raḥmān, replacing prior detailed arguments with the certain outcome.
rows.anchor: the entire discussion regarding reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier sūrahs grounded the case in reason, human nature, and evidence from the inner and outer worlds.
rows.anchor: arguments based on human intellect and human nature as well as on the world within a person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment will replace worldly standards of rank: believers with faith and good works attain honor, while those absorbed in worldly life face Hell.
rows.anchor: the values and standards of respect and humiliation will be entirely different from what they are witnessing in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–10 assert the certain arrival of Judgment, which evaluates faith and deeds and divides humanity into three groups.
rows.anchor: The Day shall evaluate a person according to his faith and deeds; it shall upgrade many a people and downgrade many

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–26 describe the foremost and the Paradise gifts and character qualities that qualify them for that rank.
rows.anchor: The details of the gifts and favours of their Lord which they shall receive in Paradise are recounted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 27–40 portray the right-hand companions’ rewards and the high character that made them worthy of their place.
rows.anchor: A delineation is made of the bounties and rewards which they shall be blessed with in Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 41–48 depict the left-hand companions’ fate and identify some grave sins that led to it.
rows.anchor: The fate of the aṣḥāb al-shimāl is depicted and a reference is made to a few of their grave sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 49–74 warn Quraysh’s arrogant deniers that continued deviation and rejection of the Prophet will bring the left-hand companions’ fate; self-evident arguments support Judgment.
rows.anchor: The arrogant among the Quraysh are addressed and warned that they shall end up with the same fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 75–96 signal the Qur’an’s exalted status and its protection from Satan and his agents.
rows.anchor: it is above and beyond the reach of Satan and his agents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are cautioned not to ignore the sublime message and thereby bring doom upon themselves.
rows.anchor: not to turn a deaf ear to this sublime message and invite their doom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fate announced by the Book is real; people should strive for the right-hand or foremost ranks, lest they join the left-hand companions in punishment.
rows.anchor: The fate about which this Book is informing them is a reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Judgment the al-wāqiʿah conveys that its occurrence is certain.
rows.anchor: refers to the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arguments for Judgment have already been given and disbelievers’ objections answered; they cannot escape the certain event, so must prepare for a favorable outcome.
rows.anchor: they shall not be able to run away from it in any way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word waqiʿatiha is a verbal noun like ʿāqibah and ʿāfiyah, stressing that the event’s occurrence is entirely doubtless.
rows.anchor: It means that there is absolutely no doubt in its happening

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat is no false warning: the event will come, and people seeking a favorable fate should prepare for it.
rows.anchor: there is not a bit of falsehood in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People must not assume their present high or low social status will last; at Judgment the standards change, elevating those with faith and humiliating the faithless.
rows.anchor: The standards of respect and honour will totally change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brief statement of elevation and abasement is unpacked in verse 7, which makes clear the standard for the reversal.
rows.anchor: Coming up in verse seven is the detail of this elevation and relegation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth will quake, leveling its structures, while mountains crumble to flying dust; al-Ḥāqqah gives a parallel description.
rows.anchor: these gigantic mountains will become dust that will fly about

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elevation and abasement of verse 3 takes the form of three human groups: the right-hand companions, left-hand companions, and the foremost.
rows.anchor: on that day, mankind will be divided into three groups

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand companions are people whose records are delivered into their right hands, as al-Ḥāqqah explains.
rows.anchor: those people are implied who will receive their account in their right hands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The left-hand companions are those whose records are delivered into their left hands, as described in al-Ḥāqqah.
rows.anchor: people whose accounts will be handed over to them in their left hands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foremost are early adopters of true religion who served it with their persons and wealth when the few supporters faced danger.
rows.anchor: people who were foremost in accepting the calls of the true religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥadīd says those who spent and fought before the conquest of Makkah have greater status than those who did so afterward, though God promises both good reward.
rows.anchor: this reality is discussed thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about the right-hand companions expresses majesty: their bliss and status exceed imagination and description.
rows.anchor: Here is it used in the former connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The matching question about the left-hand companions expresses disgust and an indescribably evil, humiliating fate.
rows.anchor: to express the opposite: hate and disgust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-sābiqūna al-sābiqūn, the second noun is the predicate; the concise repetition eloquently marks a rank beyond imagining.
rows.anchor: the brevity found in it has great eloquence in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These names do not arrange people spatially before God: right, left, front, and back make no sense there, and the left-hand group’s abode is Hell.
rows.anchor: the concept of right and left, front and back is a meaningless one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand companions are not ordinary Muslims generally; they are honored people who receive their records in their right hands and rejoice in their achievement.
rows.anchor: they refer to people whose accounts will be handed over in their right hands to honour them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinction between the right-hand companions and the foremost was mentioned earlier, with further explanation to come.
rows.anchor: I have already alluded to it earlier and more explanation is coming up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As leaders and pioneers, the foremost are rewarded first and brought nearest to God in gardens of delight, with paradises corresponding to their ranks rather than a divine court.
rows.anchor: their reward is mentioned the foremost

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is bestowed on selected servants, among whom the source distinguishes three kinds of response.
rows.anchor: We then bestowed the Book on those of Our servants whom We have chosen.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One category of the Book’s inheritors sins against itself, while another follows a middle course.
rows.anchor: Some sin against their souls, some follow a middle course

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who compete in charitable works do so by God’s leave.
rows.anchor: by God’s leave, vie with each other in charitable works

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic passage calls competition in charitable works the supreme virtue.
rows.anchor: this is the supreme virtue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ancient Persian kings decorated their gold-plated thrones with jewels and precious stones.
rows.anchor: The ancient kings of Persia would grace their thrones which were gold plated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though these verses address this community, the principle applies to followers of every prophet; 35:32 presents the same three groups in different words.
rows.anchor: in principle they can be applied to the followers of every prophet and messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foremost sit on jeweled, gold-plated thrones facing one another; this is the Paradise of the muqarrabīn.
rows.anchor: they will sit on jewelled and gold plated thrones facing one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against other interpretations, the author takes mawḍūnah to mean jeweled, like Persian royal thrones adorned with gold and precious stones.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, its true meaning is “jeweled.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutta ki’īn includes cushions, which are needed for reclining on thrones and have accompanied royal thrones since ancient times.
rows.anchor: cushions on thrones are necessary to recline against

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Facing one another signifies that Paradise’s inhabitants have no envy or ill will, as other Qur’anic passages also state.
rows.anchor: their hearts will not have any envy, spite or ill-feeling for one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verses describe food and drink presented to satisfy the inhabitants’ tastes.
rows.anchor: They refer to the items which will be presented to satisfy their taste-buds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ever-youthful attendants serve the foremost forever; this age is most suited to alert, courteous service and lets attendants remain familiar with their masters’ temperaments.
rows.anchor: these youths will forever remain of the same age

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some hold that young children of disbelievers who die will serve the dwellers of Paradise.
rows.anchor: Some people are of the opinion that the children of the disbelievers who die in their youth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an neither establishes nor rules out that view; such children need not enter Hell and may receive Paradise through innocence, without necessarily serving anyone.
rows.anchor: there is no reason for the children of the disbelievers to go to Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kūb means cup, while abārīq is the plural of ibrīq, apparently an Arabized Persian loanword reflecting Arab borrowing of cultural terms.
rows.anchor: appears to be an arabacized version of the Persian word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ka’s can mean both wine and its cup; maʿīn can mean pure water or its fountain and here denotes a fountain of pure wine.
rows.anchor: Here, it is used in this last meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise wine gives delight without worldly wine’s inebriation, headaches, fatigue, or loss of reason, which can expose a person to severe hazards.
rows.anchor: it will be devoid of all harmful effects which plague the wines of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression nazzafa al-jabbu means that a person lost his senses.
rows.anchor: a person lost his senses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fruits and bird meat are the leading examples of Paradise delicacies, and each person’s choices will be fully considered.
rows.anchor: the choice and selection of each person will be given full consideration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like worldly people, the inhabitants need a wife for comfort and companionship; houris will be given as pure, untouched partners, their features expressing outer and inner beauty.
rows.anchor: these two features of theirs encompass all the outer and inner aspects of their beauty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foremost receive Paradise as the earned reward for their deeds; an entitlement can be more valuable than a larger accidental gift.
rows.anchor: whatever they will be given, they will be given in return for their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is unalloyed bliss: worldly abuse and its harms are over, and peace and mercy from God, angels, and companions surround them.
rows.anchor: They will neither hear any nonsensical talk nor any sinful conversation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand companions’ Paradise is now described; al-yamīn and al-maymanah both identify people whose records arrive in their right hands.
rows.anchor: they are the people whose accounts will be handed over in their right hands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand companions’ garden is pictured through fruit, shade, and freshness; sidr means lote-trees, though its value may be less familiar in some regions.
rows.anchor: lote-trees do not have much significance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lote-fruit varies by region and can be fragrant, sweet, and colorful; Paradise trees are only represented by earthly analogies, and their true nature is unknowable here.
rows.anchor: these lote-trees are of Paradise; they can only be mentioned in the form of a parable in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an gives the lote-tree special importance, associating the farthest lote-tree with the Garden of Abode and Gabriel’s descent.
rows.anchor: this tree has special significance in the eyes of the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies the farthest lote-tree as the junction of this world and the next, where the Prophet saw divine manifestations; he infers Moses’ tree was also a lote-tree from the parallel account.
rows.anchor: this lote-tree is the one which is found at the junction of this world and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makhḍūd means the Paradise lote-trees are thornless and harmless, allowing fruit to be picked freely; khadada means to cut thorns.
rows.anchor: will be thorn-less and will inflict no harm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Better earthly lote-trees have fewer thorns than wild ones; the ruined orchard of Sabaʾ shows that lote fruit was prized and its trees adorned gardens, and the tree belongs to the apple family.
rows.anchor: the better the quality of a lote-tree the lesser the thorns it will have

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭalḥ means banana, and manḍūd describes bananas joined together in layers, carefully arranged for enjoyment.
rows.anchor: signifies that these bananas will be joined to one another in layers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The careful arrangement of Paradise bananas shows God has specially selected them to please the inhabitants’ taste.
rows.anchor: choose them to gratify the taste-buds of His people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Closely packed lush trees block the sunlight, giving continuous shade, while abundant water preserves the orchard’s splendor.
rows.anchor: sunlight will not be able to pass through them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named fruits are examples among many; Paradise trees bear continuously, unlike earthly orchards whose harvest may fail or be seasonal, and God will never withhold fruit.
rows.anchor: the trees in Paradise will be ever-fruit bearing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand companions have raised beds and specially recreated wives; their description follows a different sequence than that of the foremost for psychological reasons.
rows.anchor: In the case of the muqarrabīn the sequence, one may remember, is different

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wives are mentioned by an apparently antecedentless pronoun, supplied by association with the preceding beds; this concise allusion models speaking of women discreetly.
rows.anchor: a mention of wives after a mention of rugs is of similar nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an elsewhere joins images of reclining on couches with large-eyed houris, as in al-Ṭūr.
rows.anchor: They will recline on thrones laid out in succession and We will marry them with large eyed houris
